title: AI Slop Papers Published Under Prominent Academics Names
content:
Gunnar Jönsson/Getty Images
A group of little-known academic journals has been publishing “AI slop” papers under the names of professors who did not write them, sparking concerns that academics’ identities are being misused, an investigation has found.
Alan Said, professor of computer science at the University of Gothenburg, came across the journals after he received a notification from Google Scholar about a paper published under his name in the American International Journal of Research and Innovation (AIJRI).
The article, titled “Intelligence Systems Supporting Sustainable Global Development,” was loosely related to his research on artificial intelligence and sustainability, but he did not write the paper.
“It wouldn’t be surprising if I wrote a paper on something around this topic, but just looking at this paper and looking at the citations in the paper, it looks AI-generated. It has no content, it’s like slop,” he said.
He reported the incident to the journal’s domain registrar, who told him that the article had been removed. But the paper remained online and his name had been replaced with that of another individual. Screenshots shared with THE show that two days later the author had changed again, leaving three versions of the same paper attributed to different authors. AIJRI/Getty Images montage
Said also came across the American Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Innovation (AJAMRI) and the American Journal For Multidisciplinary Research (AJFMR)—two other journals using similar graphics, with the same editor in chief and board members. The former has published dozens of papers attributed to high-profile academics, including Stanford computer scientists Fei-Fei Li and Christopher Manning and Berkeley professors Michael I. Jordan and Stuart Russell.
All three domain names were registered in 2026, but the websites show archives of papers supposedly published several years earlier. The journals all describe themselves as “peer-reviewed, open access and multidisciplinary.” The websites also advertise publication fees. AIJRI and AJAMRI said they charge $200 for papers written by five or more non-Indian authors, while the AJFMR charges $80 for one to four authors or $10 for five or more authors.
“They all seem to be the same type of operation. Very shallowly written or generated,” Said said. “I’m concerned, because if a new Ph.D. student were to see my name in this journal, they might think it’s OK to submit there, too, and I would really not want that to happen.”
Several academics listed in the journals have confirmed that they did not write the articles or consent to their names appearing there.
Jure Leskovec, professor of computer science at Stanford University, is among those named as an author in the journal. “I can confirm that I did not write this paper, was not involved in its submission and did not authorize the use of my name. I was also unaware of its existence until [THE’s] email. This is quite concerning,” he said.
All three journals identify their editor in chief as Denish Brown and have a WhatsApp number with a U.S. area code. Times Higher Education contacted the journals but did not receive a response before publication.
The journals also list dozens of editorial board members affiliated with mostly Indian higher education institutions.
One of them, Kanakaraju Manupati, a postdoctoral fellow at Virginia Commonwealth University, told THE that he had not agreed to serve on the boards. “I was not aware of the existence of this journal and was not associated with it. I just checked the journal website, surprised to see my name on the editorial board,” he said.
THE has contacted others on the editorial board.

report.summary: Little-known journals are publishing AI-generated 'slop' papers under prominent academics' names without consent, raising concerns about identity misuse and scholarly integrity.
report.background: The case reflects long-running pressures in scholarly publishing: open-access fees, the growth of paper mills, and metrics-driven incentives to publish. AI tools have made it cheap to generate plausible-sounding text, while some low-quality journals exploit authors and readers by promising fast peer review for a fee. Google Scholar and other indexes can amplify the problem by surfacing papers without robust verification. In this case, three journals registered domains in 2026 but displayed archives claiming older publications, suggesting fabricated histories. The alleged misuse of well-known academics' names makes the papers look credible and could lure early-career researchers into submitting work or citing fake articles. The incident also highlights weak checks on author identity and editorial-board consent.
key_points: Alan Said, a University of Gothenburg computer science professor, was alerted by Google Scholar to a paper under his name in AIJRI. He says the article looked AI-generated and had 'no content.' After he reported it, the journal removed it, but the paper stayed online and the author name changed twice, producing three versions attributed to different people.

The investigation linked AIJRI to AJAMRI and AJFMR, which share similar graphics, the same editor in chief, Denish Brown, and overlapping board members. All three domains were registered in 2026 yet show archives of papers supposedly published years earlier. They describe themselves as peer-reviewed and charge publication fees ranging from $10 to $200.

AJAMRI has listed dozens of papers attributed to high-profile academics, including Stanford's Fei-Fei Li and Christopher Manning and Berkeley's Michael I. Jordan and Stuart Russell. Jure Leskovec of Stanford confirmed he did not write, submit, or authorize a paper bearing his name and was unaware of it until contacted by Times Higher Education.

Some listed editorial board members were also unaware. Kanakaraju Manupati, a postdoctoral fellow at Virginia Commonwealth University, said he had not agreed to serve and was surprised to see his name on the journal website. The journals did not respond to requests for comment before publication.

Said worries that early-career researchers may see prominent names and assume the journals are legitimate, potentially submitting their own work or paying fees. The incident points to weak verification of author identity, editorial-board consent, and journal metadata across low-cost open-access publishing.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the episode shows that generated text can now contaminate the scholarly record at scale, undermining trust in research used to train models and justify claims. Developers face pressure to build provenance, watermarking, and identity-verification tools, not just better detectors. For regular users, fake or misattributed papers can spread through search engines, social media, and AI assistants, making it harder to judge credibility. The case also highlights that AI-slop detection is not enough: journals, indexes, and registrars need stronger checks on authorship, editorial consent, and domain history. Without that, reputations and public understanding of AI research can be damaged.
report.tools: To follow up, use PubPeer for post-publication discussion of suspicious papers, the Retraction Watch Database for retractions, and ORCID to verify author identities. Google Scholar alerts can notify researchers when their names appear on new papers. Think.Check.Submit and Crossref or OpenAlex metadata help assess journal legitimacy and DOI provenance. Report impersonation to the journal, host, and domain registrar.
